cues.text: A fifty-five-year-old man has a sudden, severe thunderclap headache.
He says it feels like a hammer blow to the back of the head.
A gadolinium-enhanced MRI shows a haemorrhagic lesion,
A ruptured berry aneurysm commonly occurs at the anterior communicating artery,
and it presents with subarachnoid haemorrhage.
So a sudden thunderclap headache with bleeding in the anterior cranial fossa points to the anterior communicating artery.
